Day into dusk, wide, worm’s-eye from the packed earth of a Tang muster field: FOUR tall silk war-banners on poles, filling the upper two-thirds, whipping in one wind — white, red, blue, black, in that order left to right — each with a painted dragon as an illegible brush-coil, never a readable character. Below them, tiny as ants, a host of steel helmets and vermilion cloth dissolving into dust-haze. Device: the four poles as hard verticals dividing the sky. High-key pale sky going to umber at the lower edge. NO faces, NO named generals, NO Tang 唐 lettered on anything. PLACE: an open Tang parade ground, packed earth, one distant giwa hall dissolving. Vermilion is cloth on the tiny men only; the banners are the four colours. PAINTED STILL — no people, no figures, no faces, no hands anywhere in the frame; the place or object IS the subject. Sensual and suggestive by shape and motion alone, never anatomical, never explicit. A 2:1 movie frame composed for a 2:1 letterbox crop (nothing important at the top or bottom edge). Hand-painted WATERCOLOR-AND-OIL: granulated wet-in-wet washes and broken-colour dabs for sky, water and stone, dry-brush texture, soft bleeding edges and a faint paper grain; oil glazes deepen the darks and a touch of impasto lands on the single brightest highlight. Romantic-painting layout: one bold shape, at least half the frame quiet negative space, distant detail dissolving into haze. Film tenebrism: one hard directional key (sun, moon or lamp) against big dark masses, a thin edge of real light along the subject, painted bokeh from small real lights. Beautiful, luminous, painterly. NOT photoreal, NOT 3D, NOT a cartoon. No text. No watermark. DAY GROUND: the frame is built on WHITE — a high-key, paper-white ground: pale bright sky, white haze and mist, sunlit plaster and pale stone dissolving into bare white paper at the edges, the shadows few, crisp and cool-grey; the figure is the dark, inked thing in a bright frame. Never a black void, never a dim dusk wash.
